summary_html: Findings by **federal/state oversight** (CFSR reviews, OIG audits, child-fatality commissions) can initiate investigations or corrective actions that open CPS involvement.
authority_html:
- **Protect Our Kids Act (PL 112-275)** — national commission on child abuse/neglect fatalities  
- **Child & Family Services Reviews (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal monitoring of state systems  
- **Inspector General Act (5 U.S.C. App.)** — OIG oversight of HHS/ACF and grantees

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: United States District Court for the District of Columbia
key_cases.holding: After trial the court found the District's child welfare system violated federal and District statutory and constitutional requirements at nearly every stage, including a consistent failure to provide services or make reasonable efforts to prevent placement, and ordered systemic relief.
key_cases.relevance: It is the D.C. class action in which court-supervised oversight of the entire child welfare system originated.
key_cases.quote: the Court finds that defendants have consistently failed to provide services or otherwise use “reasonable efforts” to prevent placement

key_cases.case_name: Vining v. Council of the District of Columbia
key_cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
key_cases.holding: The Council may not invoke the Legislative Privilege Act through D.C. FOIA Exemption 6 (or, on this record, Exemption 4) to withhold documents responsive to a FOIA request, and summary judgment for the Council was reversed.
key_cases.relevance: It keeps legislative oversight records about District agencies reachable by the public rather than sealed by privilege.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that the Legislative Privilege Act cannot be invoked through Exemption 6 so as to permit the Council to withhold documents responsive to a FOIA request

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit
key_cases.holding: Sitting en banc the court held there is no 'jurisdictional question' exception to the law-of-the-case doctrine, so the later panel could not revisit the earlier panel's direction that the district court exercise pendent jurisdiction over the local-law claims in the foster care class action, and it remitted the District's remaining arguments to the panel.
key_cases.relevance: It is the appellate history that kept the LaShawn class action's systemic oversight intact, and it must travel on the face of any brief citing the 1991 merits findings.
key_cases.quote: the law-of-the-case and law-of-the-circuit doctrines precluded the panel in LaShawn II from revisiting the Gibbs step two decision reached in LaShawn I

mandatory_reporters: Employee, agent, or contractor of the Child and Family Services Agency — D.C. Code § 4-1321.02(a)
Individual involved in the care and treatment of patients
Humane officer of any agency charged with the enforcement of animal cruelty laws
Employee of the Department of Parks and Recreation
Any person 18 or older, for suspected sexual abuse of a child under 16 — D.C. Code § 22-3020.52(a)
reporting_details: The District is not a universal-reporter jurisdiction: D.C. Code § 4-1321.02(a) names 19 categories of mandatory reporter, who report abuse, neglect, sexual abuse, or a non-accidental bullet, knife, or sharp-object injury to CFSA or the Metropolitan Police Department under § 4-1321.02(b)(1)(A), (C), and (D), but must report to CFSA alone when a child aged 5 through 13 has 10 or more days of unexcused absences within a school year — § 4-1321.02(b)(1)(B), the District's truancy trigger. D.C. Code § 22-3020.52(a) separately requires any person 18 or older to report suspected sexual abuse of a child under 16 (both terms defined in § 22-3020.51), a call to 911 or a report to CFSA counting as a report to the police.
